events.title: The Finance Council's Number
events.body: The finance council of {parish} meets the second Tuesday of the month in the room off the office, and this month the chair has brought a spreadsheet. He is a retired bank vice president who has served three pastors and outlasted two, and the spreadsheet is good. The offertory has been flat for four years and the costs have not. He has the deficit projected to the month, and beneath it a list, in order of what he thinks you can bear to lose: the youth minister's hours, the second-collection subsidy to the mission, the snow contract, the bulletin printer, the part-time bookkeeper. He does not say it is your decision. Canonically it is, and everyone at the table knows it; the council advises and you decide. But he has done the work, and the people who did not do the work are looking at you. You can cut where he says. You can cut somewhere else and explain why. Or you can refuse to cut, which means promising money you do not have yet from people who have not been asked.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish finance council: competent laypeople, a spreadsheet, and a pastor who holds the only vote.

choices.label: Take his list as written and sign it
choices.outcome: The youth minister goes to twelve hours and finds a second job within the month. The mission subsidy stops and the mission's pastor calls you, not angry, just tired. The number closes. The council chair tells people you are a pastor who can read a balance sheet, and it reaches the chancery in that form, and the young people notice a different thing.

choices.label: Cut the snow contract and the printer, keep the people, and say why
choices.outcome: You keep every hour of every human being and lose the things that were only things. The bulletin goes to a copier and looks it. The parking lot gets plowed by a parishioner with a truck, late, and someone falls. The chair accepts the decision with the courtesy of a man who thinks you have deferred a problem rather than solved it, and he is partly right.

choices.label: Rebuild the budget yourself from the general ledger before you cut anything
choices.outcome: You spend three evenings with the ledger and find what a projection cannot: a maintenance reserve nobody has drawn on in six years, a utility contract that renewed at the wrong rate, and a diocesan insurance line that was double-posted. The deficit is real but smaller. The chair is impressed and slightly wounded. The bookkeeper is frightened of you now, which was not the intent.

choices.label: Refuse to cut and announce an increased-offertory campaign from the pulpit
choices.outcome: You preach money for three Sundays, which you promised yourself at ordination you would never do, and it works a little. The offertory rises eight percent and stays there, which is not enough. The council chair resigns in the spring, politely, citing his health. You have the people and the deficit and a smaller council, and a homily you cannot take back.

events.title: The Assessment
events.body: The diocesan assessment for {parish} arrives in a window envelope in July, computed on a formula that takes three years of offertory and a percentage that the presbyteral council agreed to before you were ordained. It is up eleven percent. Your offertory is not. The letter from the finance office notes, in the paragraph nobody reads, that a pastor may appeal the assessment in writing within sixty days, with supporting documentation, to the vicar general. You have never known a pastor to win one. You have known several who tried, and the vicar general's office remembers each of them as a man who argued about money with the bishop. The number is not ruinous. It is the difference between fixing the parking lot this year and next, between a raise for the secretary and a note about next year, between paying it quietly like a son of the diocese and being the pastor who documented, in a letter that goes in a file, that the formula is wrong for a parish like yours. Both are true. Only one gets written down.
events.flavorPrompt: The diocesan tax and the small politics of contesting it. Dry, procedural, consequential.

choices.label: Pay it and make the cut somewhere in the parish
choices.outcome: You pay it in two installments and the parking lot waits. Nobody at the chancery notices, which is the point. Your finance council chair asks whether the formula can be appealed and you say it can, in the tone that closes a question. You have been, this once, exactly the kind of pastor the diocese's cash flow depends on, and the diocese will not thank you because it does not know.

choices.label: Appeal it properly, with three years of documentation, and let the file say what it says
choices.outcome: Your letter is four pages and is correct in every particular. The vicar general grants a partial abatement, the first in anyone's memory, and mentions to two people that you write a very thorough letter, which is not entirely a compliment. Other pastors hear. Two of them call you to ask how it was done. You have become, in the finance office, a name.

choices.label: Call the vicar general and ask, as a favor, for a year's relief
choices.outcome: He listens, says he cannot promise anything, and a month later a revised letter arrives with a smaller number and no explanation. Nothing is in writing. You owe him and you both know it, and the next time the chancery needs a pastor to take a difficult funeral or sit on something, the call will come to you first, and you will take it.

events.title: The Diocesan Auditor
events.body: The diocesan finance office audits every parish on a cycle, and this year it is {parish}. The auditor is a woman from a firm the diocese has used for twenty years, and she is not hostile; she is thorough, which is worse for a parish that has been run for a long time on trust. She wants the count sheets for two years and the names on every tamper-evident bag. She wants the credit card statements. She finds, in the second week, what you half expected: a petty cash account that {@secretary} has run from the desk drawer for a decade, with a spiral notebook for a ledger, used for flowers, funeral lunches, the odd parishioner in trouble, and once, apparently, a mass stipend that went to the wrong priest. Nothing is missing that she can prove. Nothing is documented that she can accept. She will write it up. How she writes it up depends, she says, laying the notebook on your desk, on what the pastor tells her about the controls he has put in place since he arrived. You arrived some time ago.
events.flavorPrompt: A financial audit as a test of what the pastor knew and what he tolerated. The auditor is fair.

choices.label: Tell her the truth: you knew about the drawer and let it run
choices.outcome: She writes a finding and names no one, which is a kindness. The report goes to the finance office with a management letter that says the pastor was forthcoming. You close the drawer that week and open a documented discretionary fund with two signatures, and {@secretary} takes it as an accusation, which it is not, and also is.

choices.label: Install the controls this week and describe them to her as the parish's practice
choices.outcome: By Friday there are two counters, a locked bag, a log, and a policy on letterhead dated the first of the month. She reads it, looks at you, and writes 'controls recently strengthened,' which is exact. The report is clean enough. You have learned that an audit measures the week before it, and that lesson will be of use to you and is not one you wanted.

effects.value: Controls described to the auditor as standing practice were installed the week she asked

choices.label: Reconstruct the drawer's ten years yourself from the notebook and the bank records
choices.outcome: It takes four nights. The notebook is more honest than the auditor expected: every dollar traceable, several hundred over ten years unaccounted for, most of it to the poor. You hand her a reconciliation she can attach. The finding becomes a note. {@secretary} learns what you did, and it is the first time in your tenure she has looked at you as someone who protected her.

events.title: The Trust
events.body: {parish} has a trust. It was established in the 1950s by a pastor who did not trust his successors, funded by a generation that is now in the cemetery, and it has grown, untouched, into a sum that nobody on the current finance council knew until the bank's annual statement came to your desk instead of to the man who used to intercept it. The instrument is a page and a half. Income may be spent for the maintenance of the church building. Principal may be invaded only with the consent of the pastor and the diocesan bishop, and the document is old enough that the diocese may not know it exists. The finance council chair wants to use the income for the operating deficit and is looking for a reading of the word maintenance that includes salaries. The trustees want to leave it alone forever. The chancery, once it knows, will want to know why it did not know. And you are aware that the number, if it were spent well, is the roof and the boiler and a decade of not preaching about money.
events.flavorPrompt: Old money in a parish, an old instrument, and what a pastor does with a thing nobody has looked at in fifty years.

choices.label: Report it to the diocesan finance office and let them tell you what it is
choices.outcome: The finance office is surprised, then interested, then instructive. The trust is real, the terms are binding, and the diocese now has it on a list. Income may be spent on the building and you will spend it there. The chancery's regard for you rises a little; the trustees' falls more, because you told the diocese about the one thing they had.

choices.label: Spend the income on the building, as written, and say nothing to anyone who has not asked
choices.outcome: The roof fund grows by the trust's income each year and the finance council learns to stop asking where the maintenance money comes from. It is entirely within the terms. It is also a fund the diocese does not know about, and a future audit, or a future pastor, will find it, and what they think of you will depend on what they find you did with it.

effects.value: A parish trust the diocese does not know about, spent within its terms

choices.label: Petition the bishop to invade principal for the roof and the boiler, with the trustees' signatures
choices.outcome: The petition takes a season and a canon lawyer from the tribunal who has never seen the instrument. The bishop consents, with conditions. The trust is halved and the church is dry and warm for the first time in fifteen years. The trustees signed, and told everyone they signed under pressure, and half the old families believe them, and they will be at your funeral.

events.title: The Bequest
events.body: The letter is from an attorney in another state and it concerns a woman who was baptized at {parish} eighty-one years ago, moved away at nineteen, and never, so far as the parish records show, came back. She has left the parish a sum that is larger than three years of offertory. There are conditions. The money is to be used to restore the sanctuary to its appearance in a photograph enclosed with the will, taken at her First Communion, showing an altar rail, a high altar, six candlesticks, and a mural that was painted over in 1971. Any surplus is to fund a weekly Mass in Latin for her intentions in perpetuity. If the parish will not accept the conditions, the money goes to a religious order in a diocese you have never visited. Canon law lets you accept a restricted gift only for its purpose. Diocesan policy requires the bishop's permission to refuse a gift this size. The finance council wants the money. The liturgy committee wants the mural to stay painted over. The attorney would like an answer within ninety days, and everyone in the parish already knows the number.
events.flavorPrompt: A restricted bequest as a liturgical and political question wearing the costume of a financial one. The old photograph matters.

choices.label: Accept the gift with every condition and announce the restoration
choices.outcome: The bishop consents because the money is the money. The mural comes back under the paint, older and stranger than the photograph. The Latin Mass is at seven on Wednesdays and twenty people come, some of them from far away. The progressive families call it a museum and two of them leave. A bus from the tlm society visits. You have a beautiful church and a reputation, and only one of them was your idea.

choices.label: Ask the executor to renegotiate the conditions: the rail and the candlesticks, not the mural or the Mass
choices.outcome: You write to the executor about the difference between the letter and the intent of a woman who remembered a First Communion, and you enclose a photograph of the church as it is. The order's provincial, who is the alternate beneficiary, writes a generous letter agreeing to a compromise. The rail returns; the mural does not. The tlm society is disappointed and says so. Everyone else is relieved.

choices.label: Petition the bishop for permission to refuse the gift
choices.outcome: The bishop grants it, after asking twice whether you understand the number. The money goes to the order. The finance council chair does not speak to you for a month. The progressive families think you are principled and the traditional ones think you are a fool, and the chancery thinks a pastor who turns down that sum will need watching. The sanctuary stays as it was, which is to say, needs painting.

events.title: Served
events.body: A process server finds you in the sacristy after the eight o'clock, which is efficient of him. The complaint names the diocese, {parish}, and you in your capacity as pastor. A woman fell on the church steps in February, in the ice, on a morning when the walk had been salted late, and she broke a hip that has not healed, and her attorney has computed the value of that at a number with two commas. The diocesan attorney calls within the hour, which tells you how often this happens. She wants every maintenance log for the winter, the snow contract, and a statement from {@maintenance}, and she wants you to say nothing to anyone, including the woman, who is a parishioner of forty years and has been sitting in the same pew since her hip let her come back. The insurer will handle it. The insurer will want to settle, or not, on grounds that have nothing to do with the parish. You know the walk was salted late because the contract had been cut. You know the woman. You know what the diocesan attorney means by nothing.
events.flavorPrompt: A slip-and-fall suit as an institution protecting itself. The parishioner is real and not a villain.

choices.label: Do exactly what the diocesan attorney says
choices.outcome: You do not call her. She notices. The case settles in eleven months for a number you are not told, paid by the insurer, with a premium increase the parish carries for years. She returns to Mass and sits three pews back from where she did. The chancery notes that you handled it correctly, which is the word they use for a thing that has been survived.

choices.label: Visit her as her pastor and say nothing about the case
choices.outcome: You bring Communion and stay an hour and do not mention it, and neither does she. Her attorney learns of the visit and writes a letter. The diocesan attorney is furious in the way of a professional who will now have to work harder. The case settles anyway; the number is, perhaps, a little lower. She comes back to her own pew. The chancery has a note in your file about following counsel's instructions.

choices.label: Tell counsel the truth about the cut contract and the late salting, in writing
choices.outcome: The diocesan attorney thanks you and would rather you had told her in person. The written admission changes the settlement posture, and the number is higher, and the parish's share of it is higher. The insurer's letter to the finance office is direct. But the file is honest, the woman is compensated, and when the deposition comes you do not have to remember what you said.

choices.label: Read the complaint yourself and tell counsel where it is weak
choices.outcome: You read it in an evening and find the pleading error and the date problem, and counsel, who had found both, is pleased and slightly territorial. The case settles early and cheaply. The woman's attorney, who did not expect the pastor to be the problem, tells her so, and she hears it as the parish fighting her, and the parish, in a sense, was.

events.title: The Feasibility Study
events.body: The consultant comes recommended by the diocesan development office, which means he has done this for the cathedral and for two pastors you know, one of whom is still paying him. He is warm, he is prepared, and he has a slide deck about {parish} that contains things about the parish you did not know and one or two you would rather he had not found out. His proposal is a feasibility study: forty confidential interviews with your largest givers, a report on what a campaign could raise, and a recommendation, which will be to run one, because that is what he sells. The study costs what the parish spends on utilities in a quarter. The campaign, if it follows, costs more and raises many times that, or does not, and either way there is a thermometer in the vestibule for two years and the pastor's face on a brochure. He will need you at every major-gift dinner. He is very good at saying so in a way that sounds like a compliment.
events.flavorPrompt: The professional fundraising machinery of a diocese, from the pastor's side of the desk.

choices.label: Thank him and say not this year
choices.outcome: He is gracious and leaves the deck. The development office notes that you passed, which is neither held against you nor forgotten. The roof waits another year and so does the brochure. You have kept the parish's money and its calm, and you have not asked forty people the question that, once asked, changes how they look at you at the door.

choices.label: Commission the study and decide about the campaign when you see the number
choices.outcome: The interviews take a season and the report says what reports say: the parish can raise a great deal if the pastor is visibly the leader of the effort. The number is real. So is the sentence. You have paid for information you half knew and a decision you have now put in writing, and the largest givers have been asked what they think of you, and told him.

choices.label: Run it without him: you, the finance council, and the people you already know
choices.outcome: No consultant, no thermometer, a letter in your own hand to two hundred families and a dinner in the hall. It raises less than he would have and costs almost nothing, and every dollar of it was given to you personally, which is the strength of it and the problem with it. When you leave, the pledges will need a reason to keep coming that is not your name.

events.title: The Inspector's List
events.body: The diocesan insurance program sends an inspector every few years and he has come to {parish} with a clipboard and a flashlight and the patience of a man who has seen every kind of parish basement. His list, when it arrives, is two pages. Emergency lighting in the hall. The handrail on the choir loft stairs. A fire door propped open with a hymnal. Extension cords under the rectory carpet. A boiler room used for storage. The old convent's second floor, which nobody has entered in a year, with a window that does not latch. Each item has a deadline and a note that uncorrected items may affect coverage. {@maintenance} has read it and says half of it is real and half of it is what inspectors write so that the file has something in it, and he can do the real half in a month if you let him buy what he needs. The other half is what happens when a man with a flashlight is paid to find things. The premium is going up either way. The question is how much of the list you take seriously, and whether you take it seriously before or after something happens.
events.flavorPrompt: Risk management at the parish level: small, physical, easily deferred.

choices.label: Do the half he says is real and note the rest as pending
choices.outcome: The handrail goes in and the door stops being propped and the cords come up. The convent window is latched with a screw. The inspector's follow-up letter accepts the progress and repeats the rest. It is what nearly every pastor does, and it is probably fine, and the word probably is now in your maintenance file in your own handwriting.

choices.label: Do the whole list, on the deadline, and send the insurer photographs
choices.outcome: It costs more than you wanted and takes {@maintenance} out of everything else for six weeks. The insurer's letter is warm. The premium rises less than it would have. Nobody in the parish notices any of it, which is the nature of the work, and when the next inspector comes the file is thin and dull, which is what you want a file to be.

choices.label: Walk the buildings yourself with the list and decide item by item
choices.outcome: You take a Saturday and a flashlight of your own. He is right about the storage and wrong about the cords, and he missed the junction box in the sacristy that should have been the first line. You do what needs doing and write the insurer a letter that says why the rest does not. {@maintenance} now brings you things before they are on a list.

events.title: Thirty Years at the Front Desk
events.body: {@secretary} has run the office of {parish} since before you were confirmed. She knows which families are not speaking, which key opens the tabernacle safe, and which of the three pastors before you drank. She also decides, without consulting you, who gets a funeral date, who gets a Mass intention, and which phone calls reach the rectory, and she has told two parishioners this month that Father does not do that, about things you do. The bookkeeping is in her head. The sacramental register is in her hand and it is beautiful and has errors. Twice now you have given an instruction and found, a week later, that the parish had received a different one. You have tried talking; she agrees with everything and changes nothing. She is sixty-seven and has no plan to retire and no pension worth the name, because the parish never set one up. The finance council chair has said, carefully, that the office needs to be professionalized. He means her. Everyone who has ever tried to run this parish has come to this door, and every one of them turned around.
events.flavorPrompt: Firing the person who is the institutional memory. She is not a villain; she is the parish's habit.

choices.label: Let her go, with the best severance the parish can afford
choices.outcome: You do it on a Friday, in your office, with the finance council chair present because the diocese's human resources policy requires a witness. She does not cry. She hands you the keys and a list of everything she thinks you will need, which is long and incomplete. The parish learns by Sunday. Half of it thinks it was overdue. The other half sat with her at every funeral lunch for thirty years.

choices.label: Build her a retirement: a pension the parish funds, a date a year out, a party
choices.outcome: It costs more than firing her and takes a year you would rather not spend. But the date is on the calendar and she chose it, and the pension is on the books and the diocese has approved it, and during the year she trains the person you hire, badly at first and then, when she sees you meant it, well. The party is in the hall. The bishop sends a letter. She keeps her key.

choices.label: Leave her at the desk and route the real work around her
choices.outcome: You hire a part-time bookkeeper and give the sacramental register to the deacon and take your own phone calls. She knows exactly what you have done and says nothing, which is her way of saying it. The parish runs, on two tracks. It works until it does not, and when it does not, it will be because two people each believed they were the office.

effects.value: A parish office run on two tracks, the pastor's and the secretary's

events.title: What She Took With Her
events.body: The desk is someone else's now, and the first months teach you what a person can carry in her head for thirty years. The Mass intentions book has a system nobody else can read. The funeral homes call and ask for her by name and, told she is gone, ask who they should call instead, and the answer, for now, is you. Three families who were told Father does not do that have come to find out whether the new Father does. A woman from the cemetery committee brings you an envelope of receipts that were, she says, always given to the front desk. The new hire is competent and frightened and cries once in the copier room. And there is a change in the parish's temperature that you cannot measure: the older people, coming into the office, look for a face and find a stranger, and some of them turn around. {@parishioner} tells you after Mass that she visited the old secretary, who is fine, who asked after you, and who has been offered a job by the funeral home. It is the kind of report a person makes so that you will know it was made.
events.flavorPrompt: The institutional memory of a parish leaving through the front door. The aftermath is administrative and human at once.

choices.label: Spend the season writing down everything she carried: a procedures binder that outlives everyone
choices.outcome: The binder is a hundred pages by Easter and is the most useful thing you have written as a priest. The funeral homes have a number. The intentions have a form. The new hire stops crying. It costs you evenings that were for something else, and nobody thanks you for it, and the next pastor will assume it was always there.

choices.label: Visit her at home and ask, as her pastor, for what only she knows
choices.outcome: She makes tea and says she was wondering when you would come. She gives you the funeral-home system on a napkin and the intentions code and the name of the one family you must never seat together. She does not forgive you and she does not say so. The parish hears you went. It changes the older people's temperature by a degree.

choices.label: Let the office find its own shape and lose what is lost
choices.outcome: Some of it comes back on its own; the funeral homes learn the new name, the intentions get a spreadsheet. Some does not. A family's anniversary Mass is missed and they do not tell you; you find out from the sister-in-law. The new hire builds an office that is hers, and it is a good office, and it is not the one the old people are looking for when they come in.

events.title: The Confirmation Curriculum
events.body: A parent forwards you a handout from the confirmation class at {parish}. It is on the sacraments, and it is mostly fine, and in the section on holy orders it says that the Church does not currently ordain women, with the word currently underlined by the teacher, and a paragraph below it that a fair reader would take as a promise. The teacher is a volunteer. The handout was written by {@dre}, who has run religious education here for a decade, is loved by the parents, and holds a master's degree from a program you know. You call her in. She is not defensive. She says she teaches what the Church teaches and lets the children ask questions, and that the word currently is true, and that if you want her to teach that the question is closed she will need you to say so in writing, because she will not do it on her own. She means it as honesty. It lands as a challenge. The parent who sent the handout has also sent it to a friend who sends things to the chancery. You have perhaps a week before this is a conversation with the vicar general instead of with her.
events.flavorPrompt: A doctrinal disagreement with a beloved staff member. Precise about what the Church actually teaches; nobody is a caricature.

choices.label: Withdraw the handout in writing, and state the teaching as Ordinatio Sacerdotalis gives it
choices.outcome: Your memo is two paragraphs, cites the document, and is exactly correct. She reads it in front of you and says she will comply and that she is not sure she can stay. She stays, for now. The handout is reissued. The parents who hear about it divide along a line you did not draw, and the chancery, when the friend's email arrives, already has your memo.

choices.label: Rewrite the section with her, so that it is accurate and does not close the children's mouths
choices.outcome: It takes two afternoons and a copy of the Catechism between you. The new paragraph says what the Church teaches and why, and that questions are welcome, and it does not underline anything. She signs it. So do you. The parent is not satisfied and the chancery's email is answered with the new text attached. You have a DRE who trusts you and a bloc that does not.

choices.label: Tell her the underlining goes and the rest stands, and say nothing to the chancery
choices.outcome: She removes the underline and keeps the word, and the children keep asking. The friend's email reaches the vicar general, who calls you, and you say it was handled, and he says fine in the voice that means he has written it down. The parents love her a little more. The bloc that watches these things has your name on a list it keeps.

events.title: The Music Director's Contract
events.body: {@music_director}'s contract at {parish} is up in June, and the letter asking for its renewal arrived with a request for a raise, a second paid cantor, and a line, in the last paragraph, about artistic direction of the liturgy. The music is good. It is also the music the director likes, which means the ten o'clock is a different parish from the eight, and the letters you receive about it come from both. The finance council would like to pay less. The choir would like to pay more and has said so on a sheet of paper with forty signatures. Two families have told you they drive to another parish for the music and two others that they drive here for it. The contract is yours to sign or not; the diocese has a template and a salary range and no opinion. What you decide about the money is what you decide about the ten o'clock, and everyone who sings knows it. The director, who has survived two pastors by outlasting them, has asked for a meeting and would like you to bring the finance chair, which is a way of saying he would rather not be alone with you.
events.flavorPrompt: A contract negotiation as a liturgical decision in disguise. The music director is talented and has a constituency.

choices.label: Renew with the raise and the second cantor, and take the artistic-direction sentence out
choices.outcome: He signs, and the sentence about direction is replaced with a sentence about the pastor, which he reads twice. The choir is pleased. The finance council notes the cost. Nothing about the ten o'clock changes, because you have paid for it to stay as it is, and the families who drive elsewhere keep driving, and the ones who drive here keep coming.

choices.label: Renew at the same salary with a written repertoire policy: chant at one Mass, the rest as is
choices.outcome: He takes it badly and signs it anyway, because the other parishes pay less. The chant at the eight o'clock begins in Advent and is rough for a season and then is not. Twelve people leave the choir and nine come back. The traditional families notice. So does the director, who now speaks to you through the cantor, which is a kind of peace.

choices.label: Let the contract lapse and hire someone the parish can afford
choices.outcome: The forty signatures become a hundred and a letter to the bishop. The bishop does not answer it. The new director is a graduate student who is grateful, competent, and gone in two years. The choir shrinks to a size that fits the loft. The money is real. So is the silence at the ten o'clock in the first months, which some people take as prayer and some as loss.

events.title: A Business Manager
events.body: The diocesan finance office has begun, quietly, to recommend that parishes above a certain size hire a business manager: a layperson with a degree who handles the budget, the payroll, the building contracts, the diocesan reporting, and the meetings you take because nobody else will. Two pastors you respect have one and speak of it as of a conversion. One you respect has one and says he no longer knows what his parish spends. The salary is a real number, more than the DRE and the music director make, and it comes out of the offertory of {parish} before anything else does. The finance council is divided: the chair wants it, the older members want to know why a parish that ran for a century without one needs one now. You know the answer to that, which is that it did not run; it was run, by the pastor, at night, and you are the pastor. The applicant the diocese sends is very good. She asks, in the interview, what you would do with the ten hours a week she would give you back. You do not have an answer prepared, and she notices.
events.flavorPrompt: The professionalization of a parish and what a pastor does with time he has never had.

choices.label: Hire her and give her the budget, the buildings, and the diocese
choices.outcome: Within a season the reports go in on time and the contractors are afraid of someone other than you. You have the hours. Some of them go to the hospital and some go to the breviary and some, you notice, go to sitting in your office wondering what pastors did before. The parish's money is in better hands than yours. It is also in hands that are not yours, and the finance council has learned her name before yours.

choices.label: Keep the work and do it well: you are the administrator this parish has
choices.outcome: You are, in fact, good at it, and the finance council knows it, and the diocese knows it, and that is the problem. The reports go in on time because you stay up. The parish saves the salary. The chancery, which has been looking for pastors who can run things, has your name in a different column now, and the hours you did not give away are hours you do not have.

choices.label: Hire a part-time bookkeeper instead and keep the rest
choices.outcome: The bookkeeper is a parishioner, retired, exact, and glad of the work, and the payroll stops being a thing you do on Thursday nights. Everything else stays yours. It is the compromise most pastors make, and it means the reports still go in late and the contractors still call the rectory, and you have bought three hours, not ten, and spent them before you noticed.

events.title: The Principal's Projection
events.body: The principal of the school at {parish} asks for an hour, which she has never done, and brings the enrollment projection for the fall. It is down. It has been down for six years, a family or two at a time, and this year it is down by a classroom. She has a plan: a marketing budget, a preschool expansion, a tuition-assistance fund seeded from the parish, and a second-grade teacher not replaced. She has also, without saying so, brought her resignation, in the sense that she is telling you she cannot do this alone another year and if the parish will not invest she will take the job she has been offered in the public district, at a salary that is a rebuke. The parish subsidy to the school is already the largest line in the budget. The finance council's position is that the school should pay for itself, which it has never done anywhere. The diocesan schools office has an opinion, which is that pastors who let their principals leave get principals they deserve. You could not run the school without her. You could, perhaps, not run it at all, and the projection is the first page of that argument.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish school in slow decline and the woman holding it up. Money and loyalty in the same room.

choices.label: Fund her plan in full, from the parish, and tell the finance council why
choices.outcome: The preschool opens with a waiting list and the marketing brings in nine families, which is not a classroom but is not nothing. She stays. The finance council chair says the parish is now subsidizing a school for people who are not parishioners, which is partly true. You have made a bet on a building and a woman, and the bet is in the books.

choices.label: Fund the preschool and the assistance, not the marketing, and ask her to stay one more year
choices.outcome: She stays, on the understanding that one more year means one more year. The preschool opens. The families who need assistance get it and the families who would have come for a brochure never hear of the place. The number stops falling and does not rise, which the finance council calls stability and the principal calls the year she gave you.

choices.label: Thank her, decline the plan, and begin the conversation about what the school is for
choices.outcome: She takes the district job in June and the parents learn it from the district's newsletter. The interim principal is a retired sister who is kind and cannot read a budget. Enrollment falls by the classroom she predicted. The chancery's schools office calls to ask what your plan is, and you say you are working on it, and the finance council, for once, does not argue.

events.title: Six Percent
events.body: The school board's tuition recommendation for {parish} is a six percent increase, which is what it costs to keep the teachers' salaries within sight of the public district's and to stop the parish subsidy from growing. {@group_leader} has asked to speak to you before the letter goes out, on behalf of the parents, and comes with a petition and a spreadsheet of her own. Twelve families, she says, will leave at six percent. She has their names. Some of them are the families who clean the church on Saturdays and run the fish fry, and some of them are the families whose grandparents built the school, and one of them is hers. She proposes three percent and a parish appeal for the difference, which means asking people without children in the school to pay for the ones who have them, which is what the subsidy already is, on a letter with your signature. The board will do what you tell it. The parents will do what they can afford. And the number, whichever it is, will be announced by you, in the bulletin, above your name.
events.flavorPrompt: Tuition as the parish's most political number. The parent leader is right about the twelve families.

choices.label: Six percent, with a quiet assistance fund for the families she named
choices.outcome: Nine of the twelve families stay, because you called each of them and the fund found them. Three leave and are honest about why. The subsidy holds. {@group_leader} is relieved and not grateful, because the fund was a thing she had to fight for and you presented it as a thing you had planned. The board is pleased. The letter goes out over your name.

choices.label: Three percent and the appeal, and put your name on the appeal letter
choices.outcome: The appeal raises two-thirds of the difference and the subsidy grows by the rest. The families stay. The parents' group thinks of you as one of theirs, which is worth something on a Saturday morning. The finance council thinks of you as a man who found a new way to spend the offertory, and the older parishioners without children read the letter and are quiet about it, which is not the same as agreeing.

choices.label: Tell her the board sets tuition and you will not override it
choices.outcome: It is true and it is not the whole truth; the board sets what you let it. She hears the second part. The letter goes out at six percent with the board chair's name above yours. The twelve families become fourteen. The parents' group has a new grievance and a new leader within the year, and the fish fry is short-handed in Lent.

events.title: The Schools Office Recommends
events.body: The superintendent of schools and {@vicar_general} come to the rectory together, which is how you know before they sit down. The diocesan schools office has completed its review of the school at {parish} and recommends that it close at the end of the academic year, with the students offered places at two schools in neighboring parishes and the building leased or sold. The financials are attached and are not wrong. The decision, the vicar general says carefully, is the pastor's, because the school is the parish's, and the bishop will support whatever the pastor decides, and the bishop would like the pastor to decide this. The parents will hear within the week whatever you do. They have already begun, on the strength of a rumor, to organize: a meeting in the hall, a spreadsheet, an alumnus who is a state senator. They will ask you to fight. The chancery will ask you to be reasonable. The building is a hundred years old and half empty and the children in it are eight and do not know what a subsidy is. You are the one person in this whose signature is required, and everyone at the table knows what it costs to give it and what it costs to withhold it.
events.flavorPrompt: A school closure as the pastor's loneliest decision. The chancery is polite, the parents are organized, the numbers are real.

choices.label: Accept the recommendation and announce the closure yourself, at every Mass
choices.outcome: You say it from the ambo and do not let the superintendent say it for you. The hall meeting is worse than you feared. The senator writes to the bishop and the bishop writes back that it was the pastor's decision, which it was. Forty families leave the parish with their children. The building is leased to a charter school. The books close. You are, in the chancery's eyes, a pastor who can do the hard thing.

choices.label: Refuse, in writing, and give the parents two years and a plan to prove the office wrong
choices.outcome: The letter says the school is the parish's and the parish has not decided. The vicar general reads it in front of you. The parents' meeting becomes a campaign and the campaign raises money, some of it real. Enrollment rises for a year. The chancery marks you as a pastor who fights the chancery, and the bishop, who supported whatever you decided, will remember that you decided against him.

choices.label: Propose a third way: a regional school with the neighboring parish, this building, shared cost
choices.outcome: It takes the summer and a hundred hours with the other pastor, who does not want it and does it anyway because his numbers are worse than yours. The regional school opens in your building with a new name and a board on which you are one vote. The parents keep a school and lose a parish school. The chancery is impressed and slightly disconcerted, which is the best you can hope for from a chancery.

events.title: The Seven O'Clock
events.body: The Sunday seven o'clock at {parish} has forty people in it, and the same forty, and the youngest is sixty-one. It exists because a pastor added it in 1968 for the men who worked Sundays, and none of those men are alive, and it is the Mass at which nothing is sung and the homily is expected to be short. You say it, or your vicar does, and it means the first Mass of the day is over before the people who will fill the ten o'clock have finished breakfast. Cutting it would give you a priest back for a Sunday morning and the forty would go to the eight-thirty and not like it. The vicar for clergy has said, at a deanery meeting, that the diocese has too many Masses for the number of priests, and that pastors should look at their schedules, and every pastor in the room heard the word should and looked at the floor. Nobody has to decide this this month. You could decide it this month. The forty have already heard that you might, because the sacristan is one of them, and three of them have written to you in longhand.
events.flavorPrompt: A Mass schedule as a matter of people who are attached to a time. Small, permanent, and everyone will have an opinion.

choices.label: Keep it, this year
choices.outcome: The forty are relieved and say so at the door. The schedule stays as it was, and the priest who says it stays tired. You have deferred the question to a year in which the forty will be thirty-five, and you have told the deanery, by not acting, which kind of pastor you are on this, and the vicar for clergy noted the schedules that did not change.

choices.label: Cut it, with three months' notice and a letter in your own hand
choices.outcome: The letters back are angrier than the ones before. The forty become thirty at the eight-thirty and ten somewhere else, and one of them, the sacristan, resigns from the sacristy and is replaced by someone younger who does not know where anything is. The morning is better for the priests. The chancery notes a pastor who looked at his schedule.

choices.label: Put it to the parish council and the forty together, in the hall, and abide by the room
choices.outcome: The room votes to keep it, narrowly, after an hour in which several people say things about the ten o'clock they had been saving. You abide by it. The forty are grateful and the council is surprised to have been asked, and you have taught the parish that the schedule is something it decides, which will be remembered the next time you would rather it were not.

events.title: One Parish, Two Languages
events.body: The one o'clock Spanish Mass at {parish} has more people in it than the other three Sundays combined, and it is at one o'clock because that was the hour nobody else wanted when it was added. The families have asked, through their leaders and then in a letter, for the ten-thirty. The ten-thirty is the English parish's Mass: the choir, the ushers who have ushered since the seventies, the families who built the hall. Moving it means moving them. There is a third proposal, from a deacon, for a bilingual ten-thirty, which everyone who has attended one describes as a Mass in which each half of the church waits for the other half to finish. The diocese's office for Hispanic ministry has a position, which is that a growing community should not be at the back of the schedule. The older families have a position, which they have not put in a letter because they do not think they should have to. Whatever you decide is a statement about who the parish is, and it will be read that way by both groups and by the chancery, which counts the Spanish Masses in the diocese every year and knows which pastors moved them.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish with two communities and one prime hour. Nobody is wrong. The pastor decides who waits.

choices.label: Give the Spanish community the ten-thirty and move the English Mass to one
choices.outcome: The ushers do not usher at one. Some of the older families go to the parish up the road, and some stay and are angry, and some stay and are not. The ten-thirty is full and loud and the collection at it doubles. The Hispanic ministry office writes to the bishop about you in terms you would not have chosen. The parish is, in a year, a different parish, and you did that.

choices.label: Keep both and add a second Spanish Mass at nine, and say it yourself
choices.outcome: Nobody moves and you say four Masses on Sunday. The nine o'clock fills within a season. The English families keep their hour and are grateful in the way of people who did not have to be. The Spanish community has a morning and a pastor who preaches to them in their own language, and the vicar for clergy has a schedule with one more Mass on it, which he asked pastors not to do.

choices.label: Keep the schedule and improve the one o'clock: air conditioning, a choir, a reception after
choices.outcome: The one o'clock becomes the best-attended and best-sung Mass in the parish, and it is still at one. The leaders accept the improvements and keep the letter. The English families are relieved and a little ashamed. The Hispanic ministry office notes that you kept them at the back of the schedule, comfortably. You have bought a year and spent some money, and the letter will come again.

events.title: Facing East
events.body: The question has been in the parish since Advent, when you preached about the direction of prayer and the tlm society heard more than you said. Now it is on your desk as a request: that the eight o'clock Mass at {parish}, at least, be celebrated ad orientem, priest and people facing the same way, as the rubrics permit and as the old high altar, which is still there behind the freestanding one, was built for. Nothing in the Missal forbids it. The bishop has a position, which every pastor in the diocese knows without having been told, and it is not the same position in every diocese, and it is not in writing here. The choir will need to be told. The parish council will need to be told or will find out. The progressive families will call it a return to the fifties and the traditional families will call it a return, and both will be describing the same fifteen minutes on a Sunday morning. You could do it quietly at the early Mass and see. You could announce it. You could decline and be the pastor who did not, which is also a position, held at a volume you do not control.
events.flavorPrompt: A liturgical change that is legal, loaded, and read as a declaration by everyone. The bishop's unstated position is the weather.

choices.label: Do it at the eight o'clock without an announcement and see who notices
choices.outcome: Everyone notices. The forty at the early Mass divide and then settle. A letter reaches the chancery within a month, and another reaches the tlm society's newsletter, which prints it. The bishop says nothing to you, which is a sentence. You have done a small thing at a small Mass, and it is now a thing the diocese knows about you, and you will be introduced with it.

choices.label: Announce it for all Masses, with a catechesis in the bulletin, knowing the bishop will not mind
choices.outcome: The catechesis runs four weeks and is good. The bishop, who has been waiting for a pastor to do this so that he does not have to, mentions {parish} at the next presbyteral council as a model of how to do it well. The progressive families leave in a body for the parish across the river. You are platformed. You are also, now, the bishop's man on this, and bishops are replaced.

choices.label: Announce it for all Masses, with a catechesis, knowing the bishop will mind
choices.outcome: The catechesis runs two weeks before the vicar general calls. The bishop's letter, when it comes, does not forbid it, because he cannot, and asks you to reconsider, which is a command in the form of a request. You do not reconsider. The parish is a destination for one kind of Catholic and a scandal for the other. You are marked, and the mark will be read by the next bishop, whoever he is, in one of two ways.

choices.label: Decline, and tell the society why in person
choices.outcome: They take it better than you expected and worse than you hoped. The society's leader says he understands and that he had thought you were one of them, and the sentence is the cost. The progressive families never learn there was a question. The chancery hears you declined and files it under prudence. The high altar stays behind the freestanding one, where it has been.

events.title: The Rail
events.body: The altar rail of {parish} is in the basement of the convent, in eleven sections of marble, where a pastor put it in 1974 because he could not bring himself to sell it. {@maintenance} showed it to you in your first month, the way he shows you things, without comment. Now the Knights have offered to pay to have it reinstalled, and a family has offered to pay to have it removed to a church in the diocese that wants it, and both offers are on your desk in the same week, which is how you know the parish has been talking. The rail is not required. Its absence is not required. Whatever you do with it will be photographed, because the tlm society photographs these things and so does the parish's progressive caucus, which does not call itself that. Putting it back means kneeling for Communion is possible and, in six months, expected. Sending it away means it is gone. Leaving it in the basement means the Knights and the family both go away disappointed and the marble goes on waiting, which is what it has done for fifty years and is very good at.
events.flavorPrompt: Eleven sections of marble as a proxy for everything. The maintenance man has no opinion and knows where it is.

choices.label: Reinstall it, with the Knights' money, and say nothing about kneeling
choices.outcome: It goes in over Lent and the church looks, on Easter morning, like the church in the old photographs. People kneel at it without being told, first a few and then most. The progressive families write to the bishop, who does not answer. The Knights are exalted. You have a beautiful thing and a permanent one, and a bloc that will never quite believe you did not mean more by it.

choices.label: Let the family send it to the church that wants it
choices.outcome: It leaves on a Tuesday in a truck and the church that receives it sends a photograph and a letter of thanks. The Knights are wounded and say so at their meeting, which you attend. The basement has room now for the Christmas decorations. The tlm society's newsletter calls it a dispersal. You have decided a thing that could not be undecided, and the marble is where it will be prayed at.

choices.label: Leave it in the basement and decline both offers
choices.outcome: Both parties are disappointed in you in different registers, and both, within a year, have stopped mentioning it. The marble waits. {@maintenance} moves the Christmas decorations around it, as he has always done. You have kept a question open for your successor, who will thank you or not, and you have learned that a pastor can decline to decide and that this, too, has a photograph.

events.title: The Hymnal
events.body: The hymnals in the pews of {parish} are the disposable kind, replaced each Advent by subscription, and the subscription is up for renewal at a price that has risen every year for a decade. {@music_director} wants to keep them. {@group_leader} of the choir wants a bound hymnal, the kind that lasts thirty years, and has a particular one in mind, and the particular one has more chant in it and fewer of the songs the ten o'clock has sung since 1985. The bound hymnal costs, up front, what the subscription costs in seven years. It also decides, for thirty years, what the parish sings, and every pastor who has chosen one has been told by someone that he chose the wrong one. The finance council would like the cheaper long-run number. The choir would like the book. The music director would like to be asked, and was, and has said that a parish that cannot sing the new songs will not learn the old ones from a book. There is a sample copy on your desk. It is heavy. You have opened it to a hymn you sang as a child, and that is not a reason, and you know it.
events.flavorPrompt: A purchasing decision that is a liturgical decision that is a thirty-year decision. The sample copy on the desk.

choices.label: Renew the subscription for another year
choices.outcome: The new disposable hymnals arrive in Advent, as they always have, and the choir leader is disappointed and the music director is relieved and the finance council is unbothered. You have spent the smaller number and decided nothing, which is a kind of decision, and the sample copy goes on a shelf in the office where the next pastor will find it.

choices.label: Buy the bound hymnal the choir wants
choices.outcome: The books arrive in boxes that fill the vestibule and are placed in the pews by the choir in an afternoon. They are beautiful. Some of the ten o'clock's songs are not in them and the ten o'clock notices by the second Sunday. The music director adapts, publicly, and is angry, privately. You have chosen what the parish sings for a generation, and it was your childhood, a little, and it was the choir's, mostly.

choices.label: Buy a bound hymnal, but the broader one the music director can live with
choices.outcome: You spend an evening with three sample copies and a hymn index and choose the one that has most of what everyone sings and some of what the choir wants. Nobody is thrilled and nobody leaves. The music director calls it a reasonable book, which from him is a benediction. The choir leader says the chant section is thin, and it is. The finance council likes the thirty-year number.

events.title: Three Estimates
events.body: Diocesan policy requires three estimates for any contract over a threshold the roof of {parish} passed years ago, and you have three, and they do not agree about anything except that the roof is finished. The first contractor is the one every parish in the deanery uses, and his number is the largest, and his work is on the cathedral. The second is a parishioner's brother-in-law, whose number is two-thirds of the first, whose references are three houses, and whose bid does not mention the flashing. The third is a firm from out of town that sent an engineer, and the engineer's report says the decking under the north slope is soft and that anyone who bids without opening it is guessing, which the first two did. The Building Commission at the chancery will approve whichever one you send if the paperwork is right, and will ask questions about the second. {@maintenance} has read all three and has opinions and will give them if asked. The finance council wants the number. The parish wants a roof before the winter. The engineer wants three thousand dollars to open the north slope and tell you what you are actually buying, which is money spent on knowing.
events.flavorPrompt: Contracting from the pastor's chair: three bids, a soft spot nobody has looked at, and a maintenance man with opinions.

choices.label: Pay the engineer to open the north slope, and bid on what he finds
choices.outcome: The decking is worse than the report guessed and the final number is higher than any of the three bids, and it is the true number. The diocesan firm does the work and does it well. The parish has a roof for forty years and a bill for it. The finance council chair says, later, that the three thousand was the best money the parish spent that year, and he does not say it to you.

choices.label: Take the parishioner's brother-in-law and save the difference
choices.outcome: He does an honest job on the parts he bid and the flashing is a problem in the second spring. The parishioner is grateful for a year and then embarrassed. The Building Commission's letter asks about the references and you answer it. The roof is on and the money is saved and the north slope is what it was, under new shingles, and {@maintenance} says nothing, which is his loudest register.

effects.value: A roof reshingled over soft decking by a parishioner's relative

choices.label: Go up with the maintenance man and look at the north slope yourselves
choices.outcome: You spend a Saturday on the roof with a pry bar and find the soft decking in twenty minutes, and the wet insulation under it that the engineer would have found for three thousand. You write the scope yourself and rebid it, and the diocesan firm's second number is lower than its first. The commission approves it in a week. {@maintenance} tells the Knights the pastor was on the roof.

events.title: The Second Sunday of Advent
events.body: The boiler at {parish} fails at four in the morning on the second Sunday of Advent, and {@maintenance} calls you at five to say that he has it running and that it will not run through Christmas. The service company can keep it alive for the season for a number that is not small, with a warning in writing that they will not be liable. A replacement is a number with a comma in the middle and eight weeks' lead time, which is Candlemas, and it means space heaters in the church and the school on a circuit that the insurance inspector already wrote about. There is money in the account for one of these things. The diocese has a loan program at a rate the finance council considers usury. The Knights have offered to pass a basket, and you have not yet decided what a boiler basket in Advent says about a parish. The church is fifty-five degrees at the eight o'clock. The forty regulars wear their coats and say nothing, because they have prayed in colder churches than this, and the young families with infants do not come back at the ten-thirty, which you notice from the ambo.
events.flavorPrompt: Physical plant in winter. The cold church is a fact; the decision is financial and the season is not neutral.

choices.label: Pay the service company to nurse it through Christmas and replace it in the spring
choices.outcome: It runs, mostly. Midnight Mass is warm. The service company's technician is in the boiler room three times before Epiphany and the parish knows his first name. In the spring the replacement goes in at a slightly better price. You have paid twice for one boiler and spread the paying over two budgets, which is what the finance council would have told you to do if you had asked.

effects.value: A failed boiler kept alive through a winter against the service company's written warning

choices.label: Order the replacement now, take the diocesan loan, and heat the church with what you can
choices.outcome: The space heaters get the church to sixty. The school sends the children home twice. The loan is at the rate the finance council predicted and the diocese is efficient about it. The new boiler is in by Candlemas and will outlast you. The parish remembers the cold Advent for years, as the year the pastor bought a boiler, which is not a legend anyone wants.

choices.label: Let the Knights pass the basket and preach the cold church as Advent
choices.outcome: You preach on the stable and the cold and mean it, and the basket comes back heavy, and a family you did not know has money writes a check for the difference. The boiler is ordered. The chancery hears you raised a boiler in three Sundays and puts it in the column where it keeps things like that. You have used the homily for a boiler, and it was a good homily, and both of those are true.

events.title: The Letter of Assignment
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} calls to say the bishop is assigning you a parochial vicar, newly ordained, effective the first of July, and that you are getting him because the bishop thinks {parish} is a good first parish and because the bishop thinks you are a good first pastor, and you are to take both of those as what they are. The young man comes to dinner a week before he moves in. He is twenty-eight, careful, sits very straight, and asks about the confession schedule before he asks where his room is. He has a breviary with a broken spine and a car his parents bought him. He is, you realize somewhere between the soup and the coffee, exactly what you were, and you can see what he will get wrong, and you can see what the pastor who had you at his table did and did not do about it. He asks what you expect of him. It is the right question, and it is the question you asked, and the answer you were given shaped ten years. He is looking at you. The housekeeper has set a second place at the table, and it will be set every night for as long as he is here, and whether he sits at it is partly up to you.
events.flavorPrompt: The pastor receives the young man he was. A mirror, not a lesson; the choice is about how much of himself he gives away.

choices.label: Tell him the truth: the schedule, the parish's dead, the drink, the day off. Every night at six
choices.outcome: You keep the table. He comes down at six and you talk, some nights about the parish and some nights about nothing, and you find yourself saying things your own pastor never said, and some of them are not for a first-year man and you say them anyway. It costs you the evening hours. He is, in six months, a priest people ask for, and he does not yet know whose doing that is.

choices.label: Give him the funerals, the hospital, the seven o'clock, and the youth group, and take the hours back
choices.outcome: He says yes to everything because he is new and because you are the pastor. Within a season he carries half the sacramental load and you have, for the first time in years, a Monday. The parish likes him. He is very tired and does not say so, because you did not either. The vicar for clergy will ask, at the year's end, how he is doing, and you will say fine, and it will be partly true.

choices.label: Give him a fair share, a written schedule, and a door he can knock on
choices.outcome: The schedule is on paper by the second week and is fair, and he has a day off that is actually off, and you tell him the door is open and mean it and he does not knock for a long time. It is the correct arrangement. It is also the one your own pastor made, more or less, and you remember what it felt like from the other side of the door, and you leave it as it is.

events.title: The Light Under His Door
events.body: You notice it the way you notice most things in the rectory at {parish}, by walking past: the light under your vicar's door at one in the morning, and again the next night, and the sound of a television turned very low. He is fine in the day. He says the Masses and takes the calls and is good with the old people and is, at the table, when he comes to it, a little too bright. The housekeeper has mentioned that he does not eat breakfast. The secretary has mentioned, without being asked, that a young woman from the young adult group has taken to helping him with the bulletin on Thursday evenings and that she is very nice. You know what this is because it was you, in a rectory much like this one, and you know the shape of the year that follows, and you know that the pastor who had you at his table either saw it or did not, and that you never learned which. He has not said anything. He will not. The light is under the door again tonight, and you are standing in the hall in your slippers, and the question is whether a pastor knocks.
events.flavorPrompt: A young priest's loneliness seen by a pastor who had it. Restraint; nothing is said that would not be said. The Thursday evenings are a detail, not a plot.

choices.label: Knock, and sit on the end of his bed, and say that the first year is like this
choices.outcome: He is embarrassed for a minute and then he is not. You do not mention the Thursday evenings and he does, which tells you what you needed. You talk until two. Nothing is fixed, because nothing of this kind is fixed, but the light is off by midnight the following week and he comes to breakfast. He will tell someone, years from now, about the night his pastor knocked.

choices.label: Do not knock. Rearrange the Thursday bulletin, call a classmate of his, and send him on the deanery retreat
choices.outcome: The bulletin moves to Tuesday afternoons in the office. His classmate calls him, unprompted so far as he knows. The retreat is in Lent and he comes back quieter. He never learns that any of it was arranged and he does not have to. It is management rather than fatherhood and it works, and you notice that you chose it because knocking would have cost you something you did not want to spend.

choices.label: Walk on. He is a grown man and a priest, and nobody knocked for you
choices.outcome: You go to bed. The light stays on. The Thursday evenings continue until, in the spring, the young woman stops coming, and he is a different kind of quiet, and you do not ask. He gets through the year the way you did, which is to say he gets through it, and something is closed in him that was open in July, and the pastor who could have said so said nothing, again.

effects.value: A first-year vicar's loneliness seen and left alone

events.title: The Wedding in October
events.body: Your vicar comes to your office at {parish} and closes the door, which he has never done, and tells you about the wedding in October. The bride was Catholic; the groom was not baptized. The dispensation for disparity of cult was requested, and the file went to the chancery, and it did not come back, and the wedding was on a Saturday with two hundred people and a reception paid for, and he did it. He assumed it would come. It came the following Tuesday. The marriage, as celebrated, was invalid, and the couple do not know, and he has known since Tuesday and has not slept. He is asking you what to do because he does not know, and because you are his pastor, and because whatever he does now goes in a file at the chancery with his name on it in the first year of his priesthood. The remedy is known: a sanatio in radice from the bishop, which the chancery grants, which requires a petition that says what happened. The question is who writes it and what it says and whether the couple are told. He is sitting very straight. You remember, exactly, what it was like to sit in that chair.
events.flavorPrompt: A canonical error by a young priest and the pastor's choice between covering, correcting, and exposing. The canon law must be right.

choices.label: Write the petition with him, over his signature, and drive him to the chancery
choices.outcome: The petition is honest and short and the chancellor reads it in front of you both. The sanatio is granted within the month. The couple are told by the vicar in their living room, with you in the car outside, and they are confused and then grateful. The chancery's file says a young priest erred and reported it with his pastor. He says nothing on the drive back. He will remember the drive.

choices.label: Write the petition yourself and let the file say the pastor should have checked
choices.outcome: The chancellor knows exactly what you have done and grants the sanatio anyway. The note in the file is about you. The vicar for clergy mentions it at your next annual visit, mildly, and you take it. Your vicar knows what you did and cannot say so and is bound to you in a way that will complicate every honest thing between you afterward. The couple are told, and are fine.

effects.value: A canonical error attributed to the pastor rather than the vicar who made it

choices.label: Tell him it is his to fix, give him the canon, and send him to the chancellor alone
choices.outcome: He goes. The chancellor is kinder to him than you expected and the sanatio is granted. He tells the couple alone and it goes badly for an hour and then it does not. The file is his. He comes back a priest who has been to the chancery with his own mistake, which is a thing every priest should be once, and he does not come down to dinner for a week, and you let him not.

choices.label: Arrange a quiet convalidation and keep it out of the chancery entirely
choices.outcome: You know the difference between a sanatio and a convalidation, and that the second can be done in the parish with the dispensation now in hand, and you do it, on a weekday, with the couple and two witnesses and a short explanation they accept. Nothing goes to the chancery except the corrected register. It is licit. It is also a thing you and he now know and the diocese does not, and he has learned that from you.

effects.value: An invalid wedding corrected in the parish without the chancery being told why

events.title: The Evaluation
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} sends the form in April, as he does every year for every vicar in the diocese, and this year there is a paragraph at the bottom that was not there before: the bishop is considering moving your vicar in July, to a parish that needs a Spanish speaker or a youth minister or simply a second priest, and would value the pastor's candid assessment of his readiness and of whether {parish} could spare him. You could not spare him. That is not the question. The question is whether the honest evaluation, the one that says what he is good at and what he is not yet, helps him or keeps him, and whether the one that says the parish needs him is true or is you. He does not know about the paragraph. He has, in the way of vicars, begun to think of this as his parish, and his people have begun to think of him as theirs, and the funeral homes ask for him now. The form has a box for the pastor's recommendation and a space for comments, and the space is small, and the vicar for clergy reads between the lines for a living.
events.flavorPrompt: The annual evaluation of the young priest as the pastor's last decision about him. The form is small and the vicar for clergy reads everything.

choices.label: Write the honest evaluation and say he is ready to move
choices.outcome: He moves in July. The parish is bereft for a season and the funeral homes learn a new name. His new pastor calls you in September to say thank you, which pastors rarely do. He calls you himself at Christmas. You have given the diocese a priest and lost a vicar, and the vicar for clergy has learned that your evaluations mean what they say, which will matter the next time.

choices.label: Write that the parish cannot spare him, and mean the parish
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy reads it and he stays, another year, and the parish is glad. He learns, through the channel by which vicars learn things, that the pastor kept him, and he is grateful and something else, because he had wanted, a little, to go. The chancery notes a pastor who holds onto his vicars, which is not a compliment there and is not a crime.

choices.label: Write the honest evaluation and say he needs another year here, with you
choices.outcome: You write what you saw: the strengths, the loneliness, the wedding, the year you think he needs. The vicar for clergy calls to ask whether you mean it and you say yes. He stays. You tell him what you wrote, all of it, at the table, and he is angry for a week and then he is not, and the year is the best of his priesthood so far, and he will leave next July a priest, and he will know who saw him.

events.title: The Trustees' Signatures
events.body: Under the civil law of the state, {parish} is a corporation, and the corporation has five directors: the bishop, the vicar general, the pastor, and two lay trustees, whose signatures are required on any contract above a threshold and whose office was created in the nineteenth century to keep pastors from doing exactly what you would like to do now. The trustees are a retired judge and the widow of the man who gave the parish its hall, and they have declined to sign the contract for the parking lot, which the finance council approved and the chancery's Building Commission cleared. Their reasons are written in a letter that is courteous and unanswerable: the parish cannot afford it, the pastor has not shown that it can, and the trustees are not a rubber stamp. Canonically the decision is yours. Civilly it is not. The vicar general, when you call, says that the bishop does not overrule trustees and that you should work it out, in a tone that suggests he has said it before to other pastors. The judge would like a meeting. The widow would like you to visit, which is a different thing. The parking lot has a hole in it that a car went into in March.
events.flavorPrompt: Lay trustees as a real civil check on the pastor's canonical authority. The judge and the widow are competent and not hostile.

choices.label: Build the financial case they asked for and present it to them, formally
choices.outcome: It takes three weeks and the finance council chair's help, and it is a good case, and the judge reads every page and signs. The widow signs because the judge did. The parking lot is paved by October. You have learned what the trustees are for and shown them what you are for, and the judge tells the vicar general, unprompted, that the pastor did the work. The vicar general tells you.

choices.label: Visit the widow and let the judge wait
choices.outcome: She gives you tea and an hour on her husband and the hall and what the parish was. She signs, at the end, because she has decided you are the kind of pastor who visits, and the judge, who was waiting to see whether you would, signs the next day. It is not how a corporation is supposed to work, and it is exactly how this one does, and you have learned that too.

choices.label: Ask the vicar general to have the bishop instruct them, as the corporation's president
choices.outcome: The vicar general says he will ask and does not call back for a month, and when he does the answer is that the bishop would prefer the pastor resolve it. The trustees have heard that you went over their heads, because the judge knows the chancellor. They sign, eventually, after the case is made anyway. The hole is patched. You are, at the chancery, a pastor who asks for things.

events.title: The Pastoral Visitation
events.body: The bishop's office confirms the date of {@bishop}'s pastoral visitation of {parish}, which is confirmations on the Saturday and the ten-thirty on the Sunday and, between them, a walk through the buildings, a meeting with the parish council and the finance council, a look at the sacramental registers, and lunch. When you were a vicar this was the pastor's problem and you carried the chairs. It is yours now. The registers have the errors the old secretary left in them. The hall has the ceiling tile. The council has a member who has written to the bishop twice about you and will be in the room. The chancery has sent a list of what the bishop will look at, and the list is long, and nothing on it is unfair. The bishop will notice what he notices. He will also notice what the pastor shows him, and which rooms the walk goes through, and whether the lunch is in the rectory with the staff or in the hall with the parish, and whether the pastor spent the month before the visit making the parish look like what it is or like what the bishop would like it to be. You have a month. The ceiling tile costs forty dollars.
events.flavorPrompt: The bishop's canonical visitation from the pastor's side: preparation as a moral choice. The bishop sees more than he says.

choices.label: Fix the ceiling tile, correct the registers, and show him everything, including the council member
choices.outcome: The registers are corrected in your own hand with a note explaining the corrections, which the bishop reads and approves. The council member says her piece and the bishop listens and thanks her. The walk goes through the boiler room. Lunch is in the hall. He leaves knowing what the parish is, which is the point of the visitation and is rarely what he gets, and he tells the vicar general so.

choices.label: Spend the month and the money making the parish look its best, and steer the walk
choices.outcome: The hall is painted, the registers are rebound, the walk goes past the boiler room and not into it, and the council member is on the agenda after the bishop's departure time. Lunch is in the rectory. He is complimentary. He has also been a pastor and knows exactly what a month before a visitation produces, and he tells the vicar general that {parish} is well presented, which is what he says when he means it and when he does not.

choices.label: Use the visit to ask him, in front of the finance council, for the thing the parish needs
choices.outcome: You ask for the diocesan subsidy, or the loan forgiveness, or the second priest, whichever is the true need, with the numbers on the table and the council in the room.
