He does not say yes. He says he will look at it, in a room where he was asked in front of witnesses, and within the season something arrives. The chancery notes that you used the visitation. So did he.

events.title: The Anniversary Year
events.body: {parish} was founded in a year that ends in a round number from this one, and a committee has formed, without being asked, to observe it. They would like a Mass with the bishop, a dinner in a hotel, a history of the parish in a bound book, a commemorative something for every family, and a plaque. They have a budget, which is optimistic, and a chair, who is the sort of person who chairs things, and a list of the founding families, some of whom are still here and most of whom are in the cemetery. The chancery will send the bishop if asked in time. The history will need someone to write it, and the committee has looked at you when saying so. The dinner will lose money or make it depending on the ticket price, which the committee would like you to set. An anniversary is a year of meetings about the past in a parish that has a present, and it is also the one year in a generation when the old families and the new ones are asked to be in the same room on purpose. The committee is waiting for the pastor to say what kind of year it will be, and how much it may cost.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish anniversary as a project of memory, money, and who gets to be in the photograph.

choices.label: A Mass with the bishop, a dinner in the hall, a modest budget, and no book
choices.outcome: The bishop comes and the hall is full and the dinner breaks even. The committee chair is disappointed about the book and the hotel and says so once. The founding families are named from the ambo and the new families applaud them, which is more than you expected. The year has a good day in it and a great deal of ordinary time around it, which is what parishes are made of.

choices.label: The hotel, the book, the plaque, all of it, on a budget the parish will feel
choices.outcome: The hotel dinner is the event of the year for a certain kind of parishioner and loses money. The book is printed and is handsome and is mostly about the founding families, because they had the photographs. The plaque goes up. The finance council winces. The new families come to the Mass and not the dinner. It was a good year for the parish's memory and an expensive one for its present, and the chair has your name in the acknowledgments.

choices.label: Write the history yourself, properly, from the archives, and let the book be the anniversary
choices.outcome: It takes the year's evenings and the diocesan archives and the memory of the oldest parishioners, and it is good, and it is honest about the parish's bad decades in a way the committee did not expect and half of them admire. The book sells out. The diocesan paper reviews it. You are, in the presbyterate, the pastor who wrote a book, which is said with respect and a little distance.

events.title: The Planning Office's Map
events.body: The diocesan planning office asks for a meeting at the chancery, and {@vicar_general} is in the room, and there is a map. {parish} is on it, with a line drawn to the parish two miles away, and the word cluster, which is the diocese's word this year for two parishes with one pastor, and beneath it, in a different color, the word merger, which is the word for the year after. The planning office has the numbers: the priests the diocese will have in ten years, the Catholics, the buildings, the debt. The numbers are not wrong. The proposal is that you become pastor of both, with the other parish's pastor retiring, and that within three years the two be merged into one with one name, and that the pastor lead the process, which means the pastor will be the man who closed one of two churches, and the map does not say which. Canonically the bishop erects and suppresses parishes after consulting the presbyteral council. Practically he does it through pastors who agree to it, and the vicar general would like to know, before the bishop asks, whether you are such a pastor. The parishioners of both churches have already heard about the map, because the map was on a table in a room with a door.
events.flavorPrompt: The pastoral planning machinery of a diocese meeting a pastor who has to decide whether to be its instrument. The map is real.

choices.label: Say yes: you will lead it, and lead it honestly
choices.outcome: The vicar general is relieved and the bishop's letter follows in a month. You are pastor of two parishes and the leader of a process, and every meeting in both halls begins with someone asking which church will close. You do not know. The chancery has a pastor who does what the diocese needs, and the diocese needs a great deal, and you have said so where it was heard.

choices.label: Say yes on conditions: a real consultation, a second priest, and the decision about the buildings made by the bishop, in writing
choices.outcome: The vicar general writes the conditions down and two of the three are met. The consultation is real and long. The bishop's letter says the bishop will decide about the buildings, which means you will recommend and he will sign, which is what you asked for and is not the same as what you wanted. You are the process's leader and its critic at once, and both parishes can tell.

choices.label: Say no: the parish is viable, the map is wrong, and you will say so to the presbyteral council
choices.outcome: The vicar general says he understands. The bishop asks another pastor, who says yes, and the map is redrawn with {parish} on it anyway, under someone else. You speak at the presbyteral council and are heard and are right about the numbers and it changes nothing. You have kept your parish for now and told the chancery what you think of its planning, and the chancery has a long memory and a short list.

events.title: Which Church
events.body: The process has run its course, whatever the process was, and the bishop's office wants the recommendation by the end of the month. Two churches, two miles apart. One is {parish}, with the newer roof and the school building and the debt. The other is older, is on the historic register, has a cemetery beside it, and has an eighty-year-old congregation that has attended nothing else and will attend nothing else, and has said so, at the consultation, in the hall, with a parishioner who is a state legislator standing at the back. Whichever closes, its people will appeal to Rome, because the appeal is their right and because someone will tell them to, and Rome will take two years and will probably uphold the bishop, and in those two years you will be the pastor of both congregations, one of which will not forgive you. The planning office has a preference and has told you what it is. The presbyteral council will vote on the bishop's decree and will vote as the bishop asks. The recommendation is yours. The parishioners of both churches know the date, and a few of them have stopped speaking to you in advance, to save time.
events.flavorPrompt: The decision the merger was always going to be. Canonically exact: the bishop decrees, the people may have recourse, the pastor recommends and lives with it.

choices.label: Recommend closing the older church and keeping {parish}
choices.outcome: The decree comes down in the autumn. The older congregation appeals to the Dicastery and loses, two years later, by which time half of them have found another parish and the other half have died or come, angrily, to the ten-thirty. The historic building is sold to a developer and the cemetery stays consecrated and is yours to keep. The chancery is grateful for a clear recommendation. It was the practical one.

choices.label: Recommend closing {parish} and moving everyone to the older church
choices.outcome: Your own people appeal, and you are the pastor who recommended against them, and the school building is sold and the school with it. The older congregation is astonished and gracious and eighty. The merged parish has a beautiful church, a cemetery, no school, and a pastor whose own parishioners cannot look at him, and the chancery, which expected the other answer, does not know what to make of you.

choices.label: Recommend keeping both churches open as one parish, with one pastor and two Sunday schedules
choices.outcome: The planning office is displeased and the bishop, who did not want to close anything, signs it. You have two churches, one budget, one council that meets in alternating halls, and a Sunday that begins at seven in one building and ends at one in the other. Nobody appeals. Nobody is happy. The diocese has deferred a closure by a decade and you have deferred it onto yourself, weekly, for as long as you are here.

events.title: Two Parishes
events.body: The pastor of the parish twenty minutes from {parish} has had a stroke, and {@vicar_for_clergy} calls on a Wednesday to ask whether you would take it, as administrator for now and as pastor in a year if it works, in addition to your own. The diocese has no one else. That is not a figure of speech; he reads you the list. It means two Sunday schedules, two finance councils, two secretaries who do not like each other, a rectory with no one in it, and a drive you will make twice a day. The canon permits it. The bishop would be grateful. It is also, in the diocese's arithmetic, the moment a pastor becomes the kind of pastor the diocese gives things to, and every priest who has done it says the same two sentences: that it nearly killed him, and that the bishop remembered. The vicar for clergy does not pretend it is anything but what it is. He says the bishop will understand if you cannot, and that a retired priest could cover the Masses for a while, and you both know how long a while is. Your own parish has not been told. Your vicar, if you have one, has not been told. You have until Friday.
events.flavorPrompt: The priest shortage arriving at one pastor's desk. The vicar for clergy is honest; the arithmetic is the diocese's.

choices.label: Take it
choices.outcome: The drive is twenty minutes and you make it four times on Sundays. The second parish is grateful in the way of a parish that expected to be closed. Your own parish notices what it has lost and says so at the door. You are, within a year, the pastor the chancery calls first, and you are, within a year, a man who has not read a book. The bishop remembers. He says so, once, at a dinner.

choices.label: Decline, and say why: this parish needs a pastor who is here
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy thanks you for being straight and finds a retired priest, who covers the Masses for two years and then cannot. The chancery does not punish you and does not forget. Your own parish never learns it was asked. You have kept the thing you were ordained for, at a price paid by a parish twenty minutes away and by the man who took it instead of you, who was your classmate.

choices.label: Take it on condition the diocese assigns a second priest to the two parishes within the year
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy says he cannot promise and then, in the bishop's name, promises. You take it. The second priest arrives eleven months later, a newly ordained man who is now yours to form across two rectories. The year before he came was the year you remember least, because you were not in it. The chancery has your name in the column for men who negotiate, and in the column for men who deliver.

events.title: Six More Years
events.body: The letter from the bishop's office is one page and arrives in the spring of the sixth year. Your term as pastor of {parish} concludes on the thirtieth of June; the bishop is pleased to offer a second term of six years, and asks that you indicate your acceptance by signing and returning the enclosed. There is no line for what you think. Six more years means the roof you have been meaning to fix, the school you have been meaning to decide about, the staff who have learned you, the people who have buried their parents with you and will want you to bury them. It also means the same office and the same drive and the same finance council, at fifty instead of forty-four, and a parish that will, by the end of it, be as much you as you are it, which is not always what a parish should be. Priests you know have signed this letter without reading it. Priests you know have not signed it and been sent somewhere worse. The vicar for clergy would like it back by the end of the month, and has said that he does not need a reason either way, which is his way of saying he would like one.
events.flavorPrompt: The six-year term as a career's quiet hinge. The letter is short; the decision is not.

choices.label: Sign it
choices.outcome: You sign it at the desk with the pen the Knights gave you and mail it the same day. The parish does not know there was a question. The vicar for clergy sends a note of thanks that is the same note every pastor gets. Six more years. You have decided that this is where your priesthood is, for now, and you have told no one, and the roof is still the roof.

choices.label: Sign it and enclose a letter saying what the parish will need from the diocese in the second term
choices.outcome: The letter is two pages and specific: the subsidy, the second priest, the decision on the school. The vicar for clergy reads it and calls, which he does not do for signatures. Some of it arrives. You have made the second term a negotiation, which the chancery finds slightly irregular and entirely clear, and the file now contains the pastor's own account of what the parish is, in his hand.

choices.label: Decline the second term and ask for a new assignment
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy calls within the week, surprised, and asks what happened, and you say nothing happened. The parish learns in May that you are leaving and takes it as a verdict on itself, which it is not, and which you cannot entirely say. The new assignment is what the diocese has in July, which is not a choice. You have kept the freedom to leave. You have used it.

events.title: What He Will Undo
events.body: It is the last year of the term at {parish}, or you have decided it will be, and the parish has begun, without being told, to think about the next man. The vicar for clergy does not consult pastors about their successors, as a rule, and he has asked you to lunch, which is not consultation and is not nothing. He wants to know what the parish needs, which is a way of asking what you have built and what you think will survive you. You know the answer. The music will survive if the next man likes it. The schedule will survive a year. The staff will survive as long as they are not asked to change, and the finance council will tell him what it told you, and the young adults will go where the next man is not, unless he is good, and the building projects will finish if he keeps them and rot if he does not. Everything you have done here was done with an authority that ends on the thirtieth of June, and the parish will be, by Advent, somebody else's, and whether it is recognizably the one you made will depend on things you cannot see from this side of the date.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor's legacy as the sum of what a successor is free to undo. The vicar for clergy's lunch is a courtesy, not a vote.

choices.label: Tell the vicar for clergy who should come, and why, and what he should keep
choices.outcome: He listens and writes nothing down and the man who comes is not the one you named, because he never is. But the man who comes has been told, by someone, what the parish is, and he keeps two of the three things you asked him to keep. The chancery notes that you had a view about your successor, which pastors are not supposed to have, and forgives it, mostly.

choices.label: Spend the last year writing the parish down: a letter to whoever he is, sealed, on the desk
choices.outcome: It is thirty pages by June: the families, the money, the staff, the things that will break and when, the two people who must never be seated together. You leave it on the desk. The next man reads it or does not. You will never know which, and you have made peace with that, and the writing of it was the most honest year of your priesthood so far, and it is not for anyone but him.

choices.label: Use the last year to finish, sign, and bind everything so that it cannot be undone
choices.outcome: Contracts are signed, the endowment is restricted, the schedule is in the bulletin as policy, and the staff have written job descriptions that a new pastor would have to fight to change. It is a fortress and it is a good one and the next man, whoever he is, will inherit a parish that cannot be his for two years. He will resent you. So would you have. The chancery calls it a well-run transition.

choices.label: Let it go now. Stop building. Say the Masses and visit the sick and let the next man find the parish he finds
choices.outcome: The last year is quiet and you are, for the first time in a long time, only a priest in it. Nothing new is started. Some things you had meant to fix are not fixed and the parish notices, a little. The next man finds a parish that is tired and honest and available, which is what most parishes are, and he makes of it what he makes. You have built a thing and set it down.

events.title: The Man Who Can Run Things
events.body: The chancery has noticed that {parish} runs. Its reports arrive on time, its audits are clean, its building projects come in near the number, and its pastor can read a balance sheet, and the chancery has responded the way a chancery responds to competence, which is to give it more to do. This month it is the diocesan finance council, which meets monthly and is a canonical body and takes a day. Last month it was the priests' pension board. There is a letter on your desk about the parish-restructuring task force, and a note from {@chancellor} asking whether you would look at the books of a parish across the diocese whose pastor is, he says, a holy man. None of these are refusable in the ordinary sense. All of them together are a second job. And you have begun to notice the other thing, which is that pastors who can run things are not moved from the things they run, and that the pastors who are being talked about for the cathedral and the seminary and the bigger parishes are men who preach well and cannot balance a checkbook, because the diocese needs those men to be seen and needs you to be where you are. The letter about the task force asks for a reply by Friday.
events.flavorPrompt: The trap of usefulness (DESIGN 4.3): high Administration as the reason a pastor is kept where he is. The chancery means it kindly.

choices.label: Say yes to all of it
choices.outcome: You are on four bodies by Easter and are the man the chancellor calls when a parish's books do not close. The parish feels the absences and the staff cover them. Your name comes up at the chancery constantly, always in the same sentence, which is that you are indispensable where you are. Indispensable is a kind word for a wall. You do the work well. It is not the work you were ordained for and you know the exact hour each week when that occurs to you.

choices.label: Accept the finance council, decline the rest, and say why to the chancellor in person
choices.outcome: The chancellor is surprised that a pastor said no to anything and says he respects it, and does. The finance council is a day a month and you are good at it. The task force finds someone else. The other parish's holy pastor gets someone else's afternoon. You have kept your parish and lost a little of the chancery's regard, which was not regard exactly but a sense of where you could be found.

choices.label: Decline all of it and write to the vicar for clergy that you are a pastor, not an accountant
choices.outcome: The letter is short and true and the vicar for clergy reads it as a man drawing a line, which is what it is. The chancery stops calling, which takes a season, and does not stop noticing, which does not end. You have your weeks. Your parish has its pastor. The next assignment, when it comes, will come from a chancery that knows you can run things and remembers that you said you would not.

events.title: The Locked Drawer
events.body: The desk in the pastor's office at {parish} has a drawer that was locked when you arrived and stayed locked because the key was not in the ring, and it is opened now because the desk is being replaced and {@maintenance} has drilled it. Inside is a file. It is thin. It concerns a priest who was pastor here in the 1980s and who is dead, and it contains three letters from a parent, dated across two years, describing conduct with an altar boy that the parent calls inappropriate and that you, reading it forty years later, would call something else; a carbon of the pastor's reply, which is reassuring and says the matter has been looked into; and a note in a different hand, undated, that says spoke to Bishop, handled. Nothing else. No name for the boy except a first name. The parent's surname is a parish family, still here. The priest's name is on a plaque in the vestibule and on a scholarship at the school. Diocesan policy, which you were trained in, says that any allegation, however old, however dead the accused, is reported to the safe environment office and to the civil authorities, and that the pastor does not investigate. The file is on your desk. The plaque is in the vestibule.
events.flavorPrompt: Sensitive material per DESIGN 11: authored only, never skinned for outcome. The correct institutional handling is shown as costly and right. Restraint throughout; no detail beyond what the file contains.

choices.label: Report it, today, to the safe environment office and the district attorney, with the file
choices.outcome: The safe environment coordinator comes for the file the same afternoon. The district attorney's office opens a matter that goes nowhere, because the man is dead, and closes it. The diocese's review board reviews it. A man in his fifties, a first name in a letter, is found and contacted by the victim assistance coordinator, and what happens then is his and not yours. The plaque comes down. The scholarship is renamed. The family in the pews knows why.

choices.label: Report it to the safe environment office and ask that the parish be told only what it must
choices.outcome: The coordinator takes the file and says she will handle the civil report herself, which is policy, and that the parish's disclosure is the diocese's decision. It is made months later, in a letter read at all Masses that names the priest and does not say how the file was found. The plaque comes down without explanation. The family in the pews learns it from the letter, and you were the one who knew and did not visit them first.

choices.label: Report it, and visit the family in the pews yourself before the diocese does
choices.outcome: You report it in the morning and drive to the family in the afternoon, with nothing to say except that a file was found and that the diocese has it and that you are sorry. The father, who is the boy in the letter, is sixty-one. He has known for forty years that a letter was written. He did not know it was kept. What he says to you is his. The plaque comes down that week. You take it down yourself.

choices.label: Put the file back. The man is dead and the drawer was closed for a reason
choices.outcome: You lock it in the new desk. The plaque stays. The scholarship is awarded in May and you hand it to a girl in the eighth grade in front of her parents and the family in the pews, and you do not sleep well that night or for some nights after. You have done what the pastor in the 1980s did, and what the note in the different hand did, and the file will be found again, and the finding will include you.

effects.value: A predecessor's abuse file found, read, and locked away unreported

events.title: The Only Chair at the Head of the Table
events.body: The rectory at {parish} is quiet at nine. The staff have gone home; the vicar, if there is one, is at the hospital or in his room; the housekeeper has left something under foil. You have been pastor long enough to have noticed the thing nobody tells you about it, which is that the pastor has no one in the building he can say a true thing to. The staff work for you. The vicar is being formed by you. The parishioners are yours to carry and cannot carry you. Your classmates are pastors across the diocese with rectories as quiet as this one, and the ones you call have stopped being surprised by the hour. The bishop is the bishop. Your spiritual director, if you still have one, is an hour away and you have cancelled twice. It is not despair. It is the particular silence of a man who is responsible for everyone he sees, and it has begun to feel like the shape of the rest of your life. The foil is on the counter. The television is off. You have a decision to make about the quiet, and the decision is not about tonight.
events.flavorPrompt: The pastor's structural loneliness, written without self-pity. The register is a man noticing the shape of his life.

choices.label: Call three classmates and propose a standing Tuesday: dinner, no parish talk, every week
choices.outcome: Two of them say yes and one of them says he has been waiting for someone to ask. The Tuesdays begin in a restaurant that is nobody's parish and become, within a year, the thing you would fight the chancery to keep. The rule about parish talk is broken by the second dinner. It costs you a night a week and a little of the parish's sense that you are always there, and it gives you back a table.

choices.label: Drive the hour to the spiritual director and tell him the truth about the quiet
choices.outcome: He listens for an hour and does not offer a solution, because there is not one, and says that the quiet is real and is not a verdict. You drive back through the dark and the rectory is the same and you are, slightly, not. You keep the appointment the next month. It is the smallest possible change and it is the difference between a man alone and a man alone who is seen.

choices.label: Fill the quiet with the work. There is always more of it
choices.outcome: You take the evening meetings you had been declining and the diocesan committees you had been ducking and the second parish's confessions, and the rectory is quiet only when you are asleep in it. It works, in the sense that the quiet is not heard. The parish gets more of you than it needs. The thing that was asking a question at nine has not been answered; it has been outrun, and it is patient.

effects.value: A pastor's loneliness answered with more work

choices.label: Admit that the quiet is the answer, and begin, with respect and in order, to leave
choices.outcome: You write to the bishop first, then to the vicar for clergy, then to the parish, in that order, and each letter is true. The process takes a year and is dignified on both sides. The parish's last Mass with you is full. You have not stopped believing anything. You have stopped being able to live in this house, and you have said so, and no one who matters has called it anything but honest.

effects.value: He left after a long term as pastor, in good order and without scandal, having told the bishop and the parish the truth: that the quiet at the head of the table had become the shape of his life and he could not live in it. The parish filled the church for his last Mass. He kept his faith, his friends among the clergy, and the vicar for clergy's letter.

events.title: The Breviary on the Passenger Seat
events.body: You find the breviary on the passenger seat of the car on a Thursday, where it has been since Sunday, and you cannot remember the last time you said the Office as anything but a thing checked. The week at {parish} was: the finance council, the school board, the contractor, the chancery's report, a funeral, two wakes, a wedding rehearsal for a couple you have not met, the boiler man, the insurance adjuster, the vicar's schedule, the DRE's resignation letter, which you talked her out of, and the bulletin, which you wrote at midnight. You said Mass every day and do not remember one of them. You have not sat in the church alone in a month. When you preached on Sunday you used the homily from three years ago and nobody noticed, and that was the worst part, that nobody noticed. You are good at this. The parish runs. The diocese is pleased. And the thing you were ordained to do has become the thing you fit in between the things you were not, and you are aware, sitting in the car with the breviary, that a man can go on like this for a long time and that some do, and that they are the pastors you did not want to be.
events.flavorPrompt: Burnout as administrative erosion of the spiritual life (DESIGN 4.2). Not a crisis of faith; a crisis of schedule that has become one.

choices.label: Put a daily hour in the church on the calendar before anything else, and keep it against everyone
choices.outcome: The hour is at six and the secretary is told that the pastor is not available at six, and the finance council chair learns it by trying. It costs you the hour and it costs the parish a little of your evenings, because the work moves there. Within a season the Office is said and the Masses are remembered. The parish notices nothing and is, without knowing why, better preached to.

choices.label: Ask the vicar for clergy for the sabbatical the diocese offers and pastors do not take
choices.outcome: He is surprised and then he is not. The sabbatical is three months, at a house for priests in another diocese, and the parish is administered by a retired priest who does the minimum and does it well. You come back a man who has read a book and sat in a chapel and slept. The parish survived without you, which it needed to learn and so did you, and the chancery has a note that you asked.

choices.label: Pick up the breviary and drive to the next thing. It is Thursday
choices.outcome: You say Vespers in the parking lot of the funeral home and go in. The week ends and another begins. The parish runs and the diocese is pleased and you are very good at it. You know the exact hour each week when the question comes back, and you have learned to be driving somewhere when it does. Some pastors go on like this for thirty years. Some of them are the ones you did not want to be.

effects.value: A pastor running his parish on administrative competence and an unopened breviary

choices.label: Admit that you have become an administrator who says Mass, and that you did not promise that, and leave
choices.outcome: You take a leave first, at the vicar for clergy's suggestion, and in the leave you find that the thing you miss is not the parish but the man you were before you ran one. The laicization petition is filed the following year and is granted. You take a job that uses the half of you the diocese found useful, and you sit in the back of a church on Sundays, and it is quiet there in a way the rectory never was.

effects.value: He left the priesthood after years as a pastor, not from loss of faith but from the discovery that the office had made him a manager who said Mass, and that he could not be that man and be honest. The petition was granted without difficulty. He worked in administration for another diocese, attended Mass every Sunday from the back pew, and was at peace with what he had been.

events.title: The Sunday You Were Away
events.body: You were at a wedding in another diocese on Sunday and the vicar took all the Masses at {parish}, and when you come back the count is on your desk and it is down by a third. The vicar is a good priest. The Masses were valid and the homily was sound and the people who came were fine. The people who did not come are the ones who come for you: the ten-thirty, which has grown from a hundred to four hundred since you arrived, the young adults you started, the returned Catholics you brought back one at a time, the families who drive past three parishes. The offertory was down with them. The finance council chair has noticed, because he notices, and has said, in the tone of a compliment, that the parish is very much you. It is. That is the thing you have built, and it is the thing the diocese sees, and it is a parish that will fall by a third the Sunday after you are transferred, and everyone who has ever watched a charismatic pastor leave knows the shape of the year that follows. The brother priests know it too, and some of them are not sorry. You have perhaps three years here. The count is on the desk.
events.flavorPrompt: High Charisma's cost (DESIGN 4.3): a parish that is the pastor. The count on the desk is the whole event.

choices.label: Spend the years you have left making the parish not about you: leaders, the vicar at the ten-thirty, your name off things
choices.outcome: You give the ten-thirty to the vicar one Sunday a month and then two. The young adults are handed to a couple who can run them. The bulletin column is written by others. The count dips and then holds, at a number that is the parish's and not yours. The chancery notices that {parish} is less spectacular. The brother priests notice that you did it on purpose, and one or two of them say so.

choices.label: It is working. Ride it, and let the next man have his own problems
choices.outcome: The ten-thirty reaches five hundred. The diocesan paper writes about it. The brother priests attend a deanery meeting at which the vicar for clergy holds up {parish} as a model, and the temperature in the room is what you would expect. You have built the most alive parish in the diocese and it will not survive you and you have decided that is the next man's problem, and the next man will be a brother priest, and he will know.

choices.label: Tell the vicar for clergy the truth about the count and ask for a long transition when the time comes
choices.outcome: He appreciates the honesty and says the diocese does not do long transitions, and then, because you asked, arranges that your successor will be named a year in advance and will come to {parish} monthly before he arrives. It has never been done. It helps, some. The chancery now knows the parish is you, in your own words, which is a thing they can use in either direction.

events.title: He Is an Academic
events.body: The sentence reaches you the way sentences do in a diocese, third-hand and intact: that the pastor of {parish} is an academic, not a pastor. It was said at a deanery meeting by a brother priest who has never read a book he was not assigned, and it was repeated by the vicar for clergy in a tone that could have been agreement or could have been reporting, and it has now been said to you by {@parishioner}, kindly, as a thing she thought you should know people say. The evidence, such as it is: the homilies are long and have footnotes in them, audible ones; you were at a conference the week of the festival; the parish library you started is beautiful and empty; you corrected the deacon's Greek at a baptism. None of it is false. The parish is not against you. The parish is a working parish and it has decided you are a professor who has been lent to it, and it is polite about the loan. The chancery has a seminary and a university chaplaincy and a diocesan paper, all of which need men who read, and the vicar for clergy has begun to mention them to you, as if in passing, at every meeting.
events.flavorPrompt: High Knowledge's cost (DESIGN 4.3): the parish's polite distance and the chancery's pull toward teaching. The sentence is the whole event.

choices.label: Cut the homilies to eight minutes, close the library, and be at the fish fry
choices.outcome: It is harder than it sounds and you do it. The eight-minute homily is better than the twenty and costs you more to write. The library becomes a meeting room. You are at the fish fry every Friday in Lent with a spatula. The parish revises its opinion by a degree a year. The brother priest who said it says something else now, and the vicar for clergy stops mentioning the seminary, which is the price.

choices.label: Be what you are: the parish that wants a professor will find one here, and the others will find a priest
choices.outcome: The homilies stay long and a few people drive from other parishes for them, and a few of yours drive elsewhere. The library gets a reading group of nine. The sentence is repeated for years and stops hurting. The vicar for clergy mentions the seminary again and you say you would consider it, and you have now told the chancery that you are what they said, which they will act on.

choices.label: Keep the homilies and start teaching: an adult class on Wednesday nights, in plain words, on something they asked for
choices.outcome: The class is on the Mass, because that is what they asked for, and forty people come and thirty stay through Lent. You learn to say in one sentence what you used to say in four. The parish decides you are a professor who can teach, which is different from the sentence and is not nothing. The brother priest hears about the class and says nothing, and the vicar for clergy hears too.

events.title: The Pastor's Triduum
events.body: Holy Week at {parish} is yours now, all of it, and the schedule on the sacristy wall is in your handwriting. Palm Sunday with the procession. The Chrism Mass at the cathedral on Tuesday, which the bishop expects every pastor to attend and which is a three-hour round trip. Confessions every evening, because the parish has learned you hear them. The Mass of the Lord's Supper with the washing of feet, and the twelve people, three of whom have withdrawn. The altar of repose until midnight and someone to lock up. Good Friday at three, and the Stations at seven because the Spanish community and the Knights each want their own. The Vigil, which is four hours if it is done right, with eleven catechumens and candidates, a fire, a font, and a lector who cannot pronounce the Exsultet. Easter morning, five Masses. And between them: a parishioner dying in the hospital on Holy Thursday, whose family wants you and not the vicar, and the chancery's Easter collection letter, and a funeral that cannot be moved to Monday because the family is flying in. You will not do all of it. You know that on Palm Sunday. The question is what a pastor drops, and who sees.
events.flavorPrompt: The hardest week of the year (DESIGN 2.5) from the pastor's chair. The list is real and cannot be completed; the choice is what he lets go.

choices.label: Skip the Chrism Mass and send the vicar for the oils
choices.outcome: The vicar brings back the oils and the bishop's regards, and the bishop noticed. Every pastor who was there noticed. You hear the confessions on Tuesday evening and sit with the dying man on Thursday afternoon and the Triduum is done as it should be. The chancery's note is small and is there. You chose the parish over the presbyterate in the one week the presbyterate counts heads, and you would do it again.

choices.label: Send the vicar to the dying man and do everything else yourself
choices.outcome: The vicar anoints him and is with the family when he dies, on Good Friday, and does it well, and the family never quite forgives that it was not you. The Triduum is done and the Chrism Mass is attended and you are in every photograph. On Easter Monday you cannot get out of bed until noon, and the parish thinks you are on retreat, and you let it. You did not drop anything. Something dropped you.

effects.value: A Holy Week completed at the cost of the pastor's body

choices.label: Simplify the Vigil: fewer readings, no procession, the catechumens received and home by eleven
choices.outcome: The rubrics permit it and the liturgist on the parish council does not. The Vigil is two hours and a half and the catechumens are received and the fire is lit and the Exsultet is sung badly and briefly. You are at the hospital on Thursday and the cathedral on Tuesday and in bed by midnight on Saturday. The traditional families notice the Vigil was short. They will remember it longer than the catechumens will.

choices.label: Call a retired brother priest and pay him to take Easter morning's early Masses
choices.outcome: He says yes because he likes you and because he is bored, and he takes the seven and the eight-thirty on Easter morning and preaches better than you would have. You are at everything else, including the hospital, including the cathedral. The parish learns that its pastor knows when to ask for help, which is a thing it will tell the next pastor about you. The stipend is small. The debt is not.

events.title: The Christmas Count
events.body: The Christmas collection at {parish} is counted on the twenty-sixth by the same four people who count every Monday, and it is, as it is every year, the largest single collection of the year by a distance. This year it is larger than that. A family that does not come the rest of the year has put a check in the basket at Midnight Mass that is, by itself, what the parish takes in a normal month, with a note that says for the pastor's discretion. The finance council would like it in the operating account, where it will close the year. The school would like it. The St. Vincent de Paul conference has a list of families it could not help in December and would like to help in January. The diocesan Christmas appeal letter, which arrived the same week, reminds pastors that the Christmas collection is assessable. And for the pastor's discretion means what it says, which is that you may put it where you like, and that wherever you put it will be known by the twenty-seventh, and that the family will hear where it went and will decide, from that, whether to come back next Christmas with another one.
events.flavorPrompt: The one big collection of the year and a discretionary check. Christmas as a financial event, treated without cynicism.

choices.label: Put it in the operating account and close the year
choices.outcome: The year closes in the black for the first time in the finance council chair's memory and he says so at the January meeting. The school and the conference get what they usually get. The family hears that the parish is solvent and is, apparently, satisfied by that. It was the responsible thing and it was the invisible thing, and you will not be remembered for it, which is what responsible things are like.

choices.label: Give it to the conference, all of it, and say so from the ambo on the Feast of the Holy Family
choices.outcome: The conference's list is cleared by Epiphany and the volunteers cry in the hall. The finance council chair does not. The year closes in the red by the amount, exactly. The family hears where it went and is either moved or is not; you hear nothing until the following Christmas, when there is a check again, larger, with the same note. The chancery notes that the collection was assessed on the gross.

choices.label: Split it: the year closed, the conference's list, and a reserve, and write the family a letter saying exactly that
choices.outcome: The letter is one page and specific, and the family's reply, in January, is two lines and warm. The year closes. The list is cleared, mostly. There is a reserve for the boiler. Nobody is moved to tears and nobody is angry, and the finance council chair says it was well handled, which from him is the highest thing he says. You have learned that a discretionary gift is a relationship, and that relationships are answered in writing.

events.title: The Deanery Penance Service
events.body: The Lenten penance service at {parish} is the one evening of the year when the parish sees six priests in the church at once, and it depends entirely on six priests agreeing to come. As a vicar you were sent to these. As pastor you are the one who asks, and the asking is a ledger: the pastor who came to yours last year expects you at his, the one you did not go to has not forgotten, the retired priest will come if driven, and the young pastor across the deanery has said yes to everything all year and has begun to say it more slowly. You need six. You have four firm. The evening is in three weeks and the bulletin has already promised a number of confessors it does not have. The dean has suggested, mildly, that the deanery hold one service at the largest church instead of six services at six, which would solve your problem and end a thing the parish has done for fifty years, and would make the largest church the parish that does Lent. Your own evening, meanwhile, is Tuesday, which is the night the young pastor's is, and you have not told him.
events.flavorPrompt: The economy of favors among the pastors of a deanery. Small, reciprocal, and remembered.

choices.label: Make the calls, offer your Tuesday to the young pastor, and take his Wednesday
choices.outcome: The calls take an afternoon and the young pastor is grateful for the Tuesday, which nobody has ever offered him. You get your six, one of them the retired priest whom you drive both ways. The lines are long and the evening is good. You now owe four pastors an evening in Lent, and will pay each of them, and that is what a deanery is.

choices.label: Support the dean's single service and let the parish's evening end
choices.outcome: The deanery service is at the largest church and it is efficient and well-attended and none of your parishioners recognize the priest they confess to, which some of them prefer. The parish's own evening ends without a funeral. The dean is grateful for a pastor who did not fight it. The older parishioners note that Lent moved to the big parish, and that the pastor let it.

choices.label: Hold it with four and hear confessions yourself until the church is empty
choices.outcome: Four priests and a line that reaches the vestibule. You are in the confessional until eleven and the last penitent is the sacristan. It is one of the better evenings of your year and it costs the next day entirely. The parish tells the story of the pastor who stayed until the end. The other pastors hear that you did not ask them, and two of them wonder why.
